claim: Axis elongation is a conserved process in which the head-to-tail or anterior-posterior (AP) axis of an embryo extends.
source: Axis elongation is a conserved process in which the head-to-tail or anterior-posterior (AP) axis of an embryo extends.
evidence: This is a definitional statement about axis elongation that draws from established scientific understanding of developmental biology.

claim: In Drosophila, cellular rearrangements drive axis elongation.
source: In Drosophila, cellular rearrangements drive axis elongation.
evidence: This statement is supported by established knowledge in the field and is cited in the introduction with references to prior work.

claim: Cells exchange neighbours by converging into transient multicellular vertices which resolve through the assembly of new cell interfaces parallel to the AP axis.
source: Cells exchange neighbours by converging into transient multicellular vertices which resolve through the assembly of new cell interfaces parallel to the AP axis.
evidence: This describes the mechanism of cell intercalation during axis elongation, supported by established knowledge and observations in the field.

claim: New interfaces elongate in pulses correlated with periodic contractions of the surrounding cells.
source: We found that new interfaces elongate in pulses correlated with periodic contractions of the surrounding cells.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by quantitative imaging data presented in Figure 1.

claim: Inhibiting actomyosin contractility globally disrupted the rate and directionality of new interface assembly.
source: Inhibiting actomyosin contractility globally, or specifically in the cells around multicellular vertices, disrupted the rate and directionality of new interface assembly.
evidence: This finding is supported by experimental data using Y-27632 and Cytochalasin D injections shown in Figure 1 and supplementary figures.

claim: Inhibiting actomyosin contractility specifically in the cells around multicellular vertices disrupted the rate and directionality of new interface assembly.
source: Inhibiting actomyosin contractility globally, or specifically in the cells around multicellular vertices, disrupted the rate and directionality of new interface assembly.
evidence: This is supported by laser ablation experiments targeting specific cells around vertices, shown in Figure 3.

claim: New interfaces sustained greater tension than non-elongating ones.
source: Laser ablation indicated that new interfaces sustained greater tension than non-elongating ones.
evidence: This is supported by laser ablation experiments measuring retraction velocities presented in Figure 2.

claim: Increasing AP tension locally increased the elongation rate of new edges by more than twofold.
source: We developed a method to apply ectopic tension and found that increasing AP tension locally increased the elongation rate of new edges by more than twofold.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data using UV laser wounding to induce ectopic tension, shown in Figure 4.

claim: Increasing dorsal-ventral tension resulted in vertex resolution perpendicular to the AP direction.
source: Increasing dorsal-ventral tension resulted in vertex resolution perpendicular to the AP direction.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data applying ectopic DV tension through laser wounding, shown in Figure 4.

claim: Local, periodic contractile forces polarize vertex resolution to drive Drosophila axis elongation.
source: We propose that local, periodic contractile forces polarize vertex resolution to drive Drosophila axis elongation.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, based on integration of multiple experimental findings.

claim: In vertebrates, axis elongation involves convergence and extension movements mediated by cell intercalation, cell migration, and oriented cell division.
source: In vertebrates, axis elongation involves convergence and extension movements mediated by cell intercalation, cell migration, and oriented cell division (Bénazéraf and Pourquié, 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The Drosophila germband lengthens by more than two-fold along the anterior-posterior (AP) axis of the animal, while narrowing along the dorsal-ventral (DV) axis.
source: In Drosophila, axis elongation occurs in an epithelial monolayer referred to as the germband, which lengthens by more than two-fold along the anterior-posterior (AP) axis of the animal, while narrowing along the dorsal-ventral (DV) axis (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by established knowledge and visual evidence in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The changes in germband architecture are largely driven by cell intercalation.
source: The changes in germband architecture are largely driven by cell intercalation (Irvine and Wieschaus, 1994).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Cell intercalation drives primitive streak formation in chick embryos.
source: In vertebrates, cell intercalation drives many developmental processes, including primitive streak formation in chick embryos (Voiculescu et al., 2007)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Cell intercalation drives gut organogenesis in Xenopus.
source: gut organogenesis (Chalmers and Slack, 2000)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Cell intercalation drives neural tube closure in Xenopus.
source: neural tube closure (Davidson and Keller, 1999)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Cell intercalation drives elongation of kidney tubules in Xenopus.
source: elongation of kidney tubules (Lienkamp et al., 2012) in Xenopus
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Cell intercalation drives epiboly in Xenopus.
source: epiboly in Xenopus (Keller, 1980)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Cell intercalation drives epiboly in zebrafish.
source: epiboly in Xenopus (Keller, 1980) and zebrafish (Warga and Kimmel, 1990)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Cell intercalation drives convergence and extension of the mesoderm in Xenopus.
source: convergence and extension of the mesoderm in Xenopus (Wilson et al., 1989; Shih and Keller, 1992)
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Cell intercalation drives convergence and extension of the mesoderm in zebrafish.
source: convergence and extension of the mesoderm in Xenopus (Wilson et al., 1989; Shih and Keller, 1992), zebrafish (Yin et al., 2008)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Cell intercalation drives convergence and extension of the mesoderm in mouse.
source: convergence and extension of the mesoderm in Xenopus (Wilson et al., 1989; Shih and Keller, 1992), zebrafish (Yin et al., 2008), and mouse (Yen et al., 2009)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Cell intercalation drives visceral endoderm migration in mouse.
source: visceral endoderm migration (Migeotte et al., 2010; Trichas et al., 2012)
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Cell intercalation drives eye lid closure in mouse.
source: eye lid closure (Heller et al., 2014)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Cell intercalation drives neural plate elongation in mouse.
source: neural plate elongation (Williams et al., 2014)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Cell intercalation drives palate fusion in mouse.
source: palate fusion (Kim et al., 2015)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Cell intercalation drives limb bud elongation in mouse.
source: limb bud elongation (Lau et al., 2015) in mouse
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: During Drosophila axis elongation, cell intercalation is driven by polarized actomyosin contractility.
source: During Drosophila axis elongation, cell intercalation is driven by polarized actomyosin contractility, which promotes the disassembly of interfaces separating anterior and posterior cell neighbours (AP interfaces), to form multicellular vertices where four or more cells converge (Bertet et al., 2004; Zallen and Wieschaus, 2004; Blankenship et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Polarized actomyosin contractility promotes the disassembly of interfaces separating anterior and posterior cell neighbours to form multicellular vertices where four or more cells converge.
source: During Drosophila axis elongation, cell intercalation is driven by polarized actomyosin contractility, which promotes the disassembly of interfaces separating anterior and posterior cell neighbours (AP interfaces), to form multicellular vertices where four or more cells converge (Bertet et al., 2004; Zallen and Wieschaus, 2004; Blankenship et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Polarized disassembly of cell contacts is associated with cell intercalation in chick embryos.
source: Polarized disassembly of cell contacts is also associated with cell intercalation in chick (Rozbicki et al., 2015), Xenopus (Shindo and Wallingford, 2014), and mouse embryos (Williams et al., 2014; Lau et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Polarized disassembly of cell contacts is associated with cell intercalation in Xenopus embryos.
source: Polarized disassembly of cell contacts is also associated with cell intercalation in chick (Rozbicki et al., 2015), Xenopus (Shindo and Wallingford, 2014), and mouse embryos (Williams et al., 2014; Lau et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Polarized disassembly of cell contacts is associated with cell intercalation in mouse embryos.
source: Polarized disassembly of cell contacts is also associated with cell intercalation in chick (Rozbicki et al., 2015), Xenopus (Shindo and Wallingford, 2014), and mouse embryos (Williams et al., 2014; Lau et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Following contraction of AP interfaces in the Drosophila germband, multicellular vertices are systematically resolved through the assembly of new contacts separating dorsal and ventral cell neighbours.
source: Following contraction of AP interfaces in the Drosophila germband, multicellular vertices are systematically resolved through the assembly of new contacts separating dorsal and ventral cell neighbours (DV interfaces, Figure 1—figure supplement 1B, Video 1).
evidence: This is supported by established knowledge and visual evidence in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B and Video 1.

claim: Myosin turnover between phosphorylated and unphosphorylated states is important for the directionality of vertex resolution.
source: Myosin turnover between phosphorylated and unphosphorylated states is important for the directionality of vertex resolution (Kasza et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Computational modelling predicts that periodic contraction of the apical surface of germband cells, driven by pulsatile actomyosin networks, could promote the oriented assembly of new cell contacts.
source: Computational modelling suggests that periodic contraction of the apical surface of germband cells, driven by pulsatile actomyosin networks, could promote the oriented assembly of new cell contacts (Lan et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior computational modeling work.

claim: The assembly of new DV edges occurred in cycles of elongation and shortening with a period of 126 ± 5 s.
source: We found that the assembly of new DV edges occurred in cycles of elongation and shortening (Figure 1A–B, blue line), with a period of 126 ± 5 s (n = 110 edges).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the study supported by data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Elongation pulses increased edge length by 772 ± 46 nm on average.
source: On average, elongation pulses increased edge length by 772 ± 46 nm, while shortening pulses decreased edge length by a significantly smaller amount, 114 ± 19 nm (n = 110 edges, p = 9.0 × 10−22), thus resulting in net edge elongation.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the study with statistical analysis.

claim: Shortening pulses decreased edge length by 114 ± 19 nm on average.
source: On average, elongation pulses increased edge length by 772 ± 46 nm, while shortening pulses decreased edge length by a significantly smaller amount, 114 ± 19 nm (n = 110 edges, p = 9.0 × 10−22), thus resulting in net edge elongation.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the study with statistical analysis.

claim: Shortening pulses decreased edge length by a significantly smaller amount than elongation pulses increased it.
source: On average, elongation pulses increased edge length by 772 ± 46 nm, while shortening pulses decreased edge length by a significantly smaller amount, 114 ± 19 nm (n = 110 edges, p = 9.0 × 10−22), thus resulting in net edge elongation.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the study with statistical analysis (p = 9.0 × 10−22).

claim: Germband cells undergo characteristic cycles of apical area contraction and relaxation with a period of 130 ± 3 s.
source: Germband cells undergo characteristic cycles of apical area contraction and relaxation with a period of 130 ± 3 s, and predominantly oriented along the AP axis of the embryo (Fernandez-Gonzalez and Zallen, 2011; Sawyer et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Germband cell apical area oscillations are predominantly oriented along the AP axis of the embryo.
source: Germband cells undergo characteristic cycles of apical area contraction and relaxation with a period of 130 ± 3 s, and predominantly oriented along the AP axis of the embryo (Fernandez-Gonzalez and Zallen, 2011; Sawyer et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: In 65% of cases (143/220 cell-edge pairs), there was a negative correlation between changes in length of the new DV junction and changes in area of the cell anterior or posterior to it.
source: In a majority of cases (143/220 cell-edge pairs, 65%), we observed a negative correlation between changes in length of the new DV junction and changes in area of the cell anterior or posterior to it (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the study supported by data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Short time shifts of the edge length signal maximized the anti-correlation between edge length and anterior/posterior cell area changes.
source: We found that short time shifts of the edge length signal maximized the anti-correlation, while longer time shifts were necessary to maximize the correlation (p = 1.74 × 10−5, Figure 1D–E)
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the study with statistical analysis, supported by data in Figure 1D-E.

claim: Longer time shifts were necessary to maximize the correlation between edge length and anterior/posterior cell area changes.
source: We found that short time shifts of the edge length signal maximized the anti-correlation, while longer time shifts were necessary to maximize the correlation (p = 1.74 × 10−5, Figure 1D–E)
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the study with statistical analysis, supported by data in Figure 1D-E.

claim: Changes in length of the new edge were predominantly positively correlated with changes in the apical area of the dorsal and ventral cells in 71% of cases (156/220 cell-edge pairs).
source: Similar analyses demonstrated that changes in length of the new edge were predominantly positively correlated with changes in the apical area of the dorsal and ventral cells, which share the new edge (156/220 cell-edge pairs, 71%, Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the study supported by data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Pulsed contractions of the cells in the immediate vicinity of a multicellular vertex may promote vertex resolution during Drosophila axis elongation.
source: Together, our results suggest that pulsed contractions of the cells in the immediate vicinity of a multicellular vertex may promote vertex resolution during Drosophila axis elongation.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the correlation analyses between edge elongation and cell area changes.

claim: The cyclical changes of apical area in germband cells are driven by pulsatile networks of medial-apical non-muscle myosin II.
source: The cyclical changes of apical area in germband cells are driven by pulsatile networks of medial-apical non-muscle myosin II (Rauzi et al., 2010; Fernandez-Gonzalez and Zallen, 2011; Sawyer et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Rho-kinase is one of the main activators of myosin.
source: Rho-kinase is one of the main activators of myosin (Amano et al., 1996; Kimura et al., 1996)
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Treatment with Y-27632 abolishes the ability of germband cells to generate mechanical force.
source: Rho-kinase is one of the main activators of myosin (Amano et al., 1996; Kimura et al., 1996), and treatment with Y-27632 abolishes the ability of germband cells to generate mechanical force (Fernandez-Gonzalez et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: In Y-27632-injected embryos, germband cells displayed a rapid loss of myosin from their apical surface.
source: In Y-27632-injected embryos, germband cells displayed a rapid loss of myosin from their apical surface (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A)
evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by data in Figure 1—figure supplement 3A.

claim: Y-27632 injection resulted in a dramatic reduction in the amplitude of apical area oscillation.
source: In Y-27632-injected embryos, germband cells displayed a rapid loss of myosin from their apical surface (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A), resulting in a dramatic reduction in the amplitude of apical area oscillation (p = 1.7 × 10−44, Figure 1F–H).
evidence: This is an experimental finding with statistical analysis, supported by data in Figure 1F-H.

claim: 9/25 vertices resolved within 30° of the DV axis in Y-27632-injected embryos, in contrast to 0/28 in water-injected controls.
source: Inhibiting actomyosin contractility affected the directionality of vertex resolution: 9/25 vertices resolved within 30° of the DV axis in Y-27632-injected embryos, in contrast to 0/28 in water-injected controls (p = 0.02, Figure 1I,J',K, Video 2).
evidence: This is an experimental finding with statistical analysis, supported by data in Figure 1I,J',K and Video 2.

claim: Inhibiting Rho-kinase reduced the rate of new edge elongation from 0.28 ± 0.06 μm/min in controls to 0.001 ± 0.080 μm/min for vertices that resolved along the AP axis.
source: In addition, for vertices that resolved along the AP axis, inhibiting Rho-kinase reduced the rate of new edge elongation with respect to controls (0.001 ± 0.080 μm/min vs. 0.28 ± 0.06 μm/min, respectively, p = 0.01, Figure 1I,J,L, Video 2)
evidence: This is an experimental finding with statistical analysis, supported by data in Figure 1I,J,L and Video 2.

claim: Myosin activity facilitates the assembly of new DV interfaces.
source: In addition, for vertices that resolved along the AP axis, inhibiting Rho-kinase reduced the rate of new edge elongation with respect to controls (0.001 ± 0.080 μm/min vs. 0.28 ± 0.06 μm/min, respectively, p = 0.01, Figure 1I,J,L, Video 2), suggesting that myosin activity facilitates the assembly of new DV interfaces.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental results showing reduced edge elongation upon Rho-kinase inhibition.

claim: Rho-kinase activity can regulate the localization of the Par polarity complex.
source: However, Rho-kinase activity can regulate the localization of the Par polarity complex (Atwood and Prehoda, 2009; Simões et al., 2010) (Figure 1—figure supplement 4A)
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work and data in Figure 1—figure supplement 4A.

claim: Cytochalasin D blocks actin polymerization by binding to the elongating end of filaments and preventing the addition of new actin monomers.
source: To further investigate the role of mechanical forces in vertex resolution, we disrupted actomyosin contractility by injecting embryos with 5 mM of Cytochalasin D, a drug that blocks actin polymerization by binding to the elongating end of filaments and preventing the addition of new actin monomers (Flanagan and Lin, 1980).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work describing the mechanism of Cytochalasin D.

claim: Cytochalasin D injection disrupted the actin cytoskeleton.
source: Cytochalasin D injection disrupted the actin cytoskeleton (Figure 1—figure supplement 5A–B)
evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by data in Figure 1—figure supplement 5A-B.

claim: Cytochalasin D injection reduced apical area oscillations.
source: Cytochalasin D injection disrupted the actin cytoskeleton (Figure 1—figure supplement 5A–B) and reduced apical area oscillations (p = 0.04, Figure 1—figure supplement 5C–E)
evidence: This is an experimental finding with statistical analysis, supported by data in Figure 1—figure supplement 5C-E.

claim: Cytochalasin D treatment did not affect the localization of Par-6, a member of the Par complex.
source: Cytochalasin D injection disrupted the actin cytoskeleton (Figure 1—figure supplement 5A–B) and reduced apical area oscillations (p = 0.04, Figure 1—figure supplement 5C–E), without affecting the localization of Par-6, a member of the Par complex (Figure 1—figure supplement 4B).
evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by data in Figure 1—figure supplement 4B.

claim: Cytochalasin D treatment led to an 83% reduction in the rate of new DV edge assembly with respect to controls.
source: Cytochalasin D treatment led to an 83% reduction in the rate of new DV edge assembly with respect to controls (0.07 ± 0.10 μm/min vs. 0.40 ± 0.05 μm/min, respectively, p = 0.01, Figure 1—figure supplement 5F–G,J, Video 3).
evidence: This is an experimental finding with statistical analysis, supported by data in Figure 1—figure supplement 5F-G,J and Video 3.

claim: In Cytochalasin D-injected embryos 4/15 vertices resolved along the DV axis, in contrast to 0/50 in DMSO-injected controls.
source: In Cytochalasin D-injected embryos 4/15 vertices resolved along the DV axis, in contrast to 0/50 in DMSO-injected controls (p = 4.0 × 10−15, Figure 1—figure supplement 5F,H–I, Video 3).
evidence: This is an experimental finding with statistical analysis, supported by data in Figure 1—figure supplement 5F,H-I and Video 3.

claim: In Cytochalasin D-injected embryos, 32/47 vertices persisted for at least 10 min and up to 40 min.
source: Strikingly, in Cytochalasin D-injected embryos, 32/47 vertices persisted for at least 10 min and up to 40 min (Figure 1—figure supplement 5K).
evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by data in Figure 1—figure supplement 5K.

claim: Actomyosin contractility is necessary for the directional assembly of new interfaces during vertex resolution in Drosophila axis elongation.
source: Together, our results demonstrate that actomyosin contractility is necessary for the directional assembly of new interfaces during vertex resolution in Drosophila axis elongation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the Y-27632 and Cytochalasin D experiments.

claim: The instantaneous retraction velocity of vertices after laser ablation is proportional to the tension sustained by the interface prior to ablation.
source: The instantaneous retraction velocity of the vertices is proportional to the tension sustained by the interface prior to ablation (Hutson et al., 2003; Fernandez-Gonzalez et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work establishing this relationship.

claim: The retraction velocity after ablation of new DV junctions was 0.81 ± 0.08 μm/s, 32% greater than the retraction velocity after severing control DV edges (0.61 ± 0.03 μm/s).
source: The retraction velocity after ablation of new DV junctions was 0.81 ± 0.08 μm/s, 32% greater than the retraction velocity after severing control DV edges (0.61 ± 0.03 μm/s, p = 0.05, Figure 2C)
evidence: This is an experimental finding with statistical analysis, supported by data in Figure 2C.

claim: New DV edges sustain increased mechanical tension with respect to non-elongating edges with similar orientation, assuming uniform viscoelastic properties.
source: The retraction velocity after ablation of new DV junctions was 0.81 ± 0.08 μm/s, 32% greater than the retraction velocity after severing control DV edges (0.61 ± 0.03 μm/s, p = 0.05, Figure 2C), indicating that – assuming uniform viscoelastic properties – new DV edges sustain increased mechanical tension with respect to non-elongating edges with similar orientation.
evidence: This is an inference from the laser ablation data, with the caveat about uniform viscoelastic properties.

claim: New DV interfaces displayed smaller angles between the anterior or posterior cell junctions (θavg = 136.6 ± 3.3°) than control DV interfaces (θavg = 150.3 ± 3.4°).
source: New DV interfaces displayed smaller angles between the anterior or posterior cell junctions (θavg = 136.6 ± 3.3°) than control DV interfaces, (θavg = 150.3 ± 3.4°, p = 0.02, Figure 2A–B,D)
evidence: This is an experimental finding with statistical analysis, supported by data in Figure 2A-B,D.

claim: The retraction velocity after laser ablation was significantly anti-correlated with the angle between the anterior or posterior cell junctions (r = −0.6).
source: New DV interfaces displayed smaller angles between the anterior or posterior cell junctions (θavg = 136.6 ± 3.3°) than control DV interfaces, (θavg = 150.3 ± 3.4°, p = 0.02, Figure 2A–B,D), and the retraction velocity after laser ablation was significantly anti-correlated with the angle between the anterior or posterior cell junctions (r = −0.6, p = 2.9 × 10−5).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from correlation analysis of the experimental data.

claim: No correlation was found between control or new DV interface length and instantaneous retraction velocity after ablation.
source: Notably, no correlation was found between control or new DV interface length and instantaneous retraction velocity after ablation (r = 0.04 and 0.35, respectively, Figure 2E,F and Figure 2—figure supplement 1)
evidence: This is a statistical finding from correlation analysis, supported by data in Figure 2E,F and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Differences in retraction velocity between control and new DV edges are independent from interface length, and determined by whether the edge is being assembled.
source: Notably, no correlation was found between control or new DV interface length and instantaneous retraction velocity after ablation (r = 0.04 and 0.35, respectively, Figure 2E,F and Figure 2—figure supplement 1), suggesting that differences in retraction velocity between control and new DV edges are independent from interface length, and determined by whether the edge is being assembled.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the lack of correlation between interface length and retraction velocity.

claim: New DV edges were myosin-depleted.
source: New DV edges were myosin-depleted (Blankenship et al., 2006) (p = 4.3 × 10−5, Figure 2—figure supplement 2)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work and confirmed by data in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Vertex retraction after ablation of new DV edges was caused by tension generated elsewhere and exerted onto the new edge.
source: New DV edges were myosin-depleted (Blankenship et al., 2006) (p = 4.3 × 10−5, Figure 2—figure supplement 2), suggesting that vertex retraction after ablation of new DV edges was caused by tension generated elsewhere and exerted onto the new edge.
evidence: This is an inference from the observation that new DV edges lack myosin but still retract after ablation.

claim: Mechanical tension parallel to the AP axis of the embryo contributes to vertex resolution.
source: Together, our data strongly suggest that mechanical tension parallel to the AP axis of the embryo contributes to vertex resolution.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the laser ablation experiments showing increased tension in new DV edges.

claim: When the contractile activity of anterior/posterior cells was disrupted, 4/7 four-cell vertices did not resolve, in contrast to 0/10 vertices in sham-irradiated controls.
source: When the contractile activity of anterior/posterior cells was disrupted, 4/7 four-cell vertices did not resolve (their length was never greater than 1 μm for at least 1 min), in contrast to 0/10 vertices in sham-irradiated controls.
evidence: This is an experimental finding from targeted laser ablation experiments.

claim: In controls, the rate of new edge elongation calculated over 180 s was 0.47 ± 0.08 μm/min.
source: In controls, the rate of new edge elongation calculated over 180 s was 0.47 ± 0.08 μm/min (Figure 3A,C).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from control experiments, supported by data in Figure 3A,C.

claim: Preventing contraction of the anterior/posterior cells resulted in a significant reduction of the rate of new edge elongation to 0.18 ± 0.05 μm/min for the vertices that resolved.
source: Preventing contraction of the anterior/posterior cells resulted in a significant reduction of the rate of new edge elongation to 0.18 ± 0.05 μm/min for the vertices that resolved (p = 0.03; Figure 3B–C).
evidence: This is an experimental finding with statistical analysis, supported by data in Figure 3B-C.

claim: Contractility in the cells anterior and posterior to a multicellular vertex is necessary for vertex resolution and the assembly of the new DV interface.
source: These results suggest that contractility in the cells anterior and posterior to a multicellular vertex is necessary for vertex resolution and the assembly of the new DV interface.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experiments disrupting contractility in anterior/posterior cells.

claim: When contraction of the DV cells was disrupted, 5/7 new DV interfaces reached a length of at least 1 μm, similar to 10/10 in controls.
source: In contrast with the ablation of anterior/posterior cells, ablation of the DV cells did not prevent vertex resolution: 5/7 new DV interfaces reached a length of at least 1 μm, similar to 10/10 in controls.
evidence: This is an experimental finding from targeted laser ablation experiments.

claim: The initial rates of elongation were similar when contraction of the DV cells was disrupted (0.37 ± 0.11 µm/min over 60 s) compared to sham-irradiated controls (0.50 ± 0.15 µm/min).
source: The initial rates of elongation were similar, with new DV interfaces elongating at a rate of 0.37 ± 0.11 µm/min over 60 s when contraction of the DV cells was disrupted, compared to rates of 0.50 ± 0.15 µm/min in sham-irradiated controls (p = 0.48, Figure 3D–F).
evidence: This is an experimental finding with statistical analysis, supported by data in Figure 3D-F.

claim: Ablation of the dorsal and ventral cells resulted in a significant reduction of the rate of new interface elongation over the subsequent 120 s of elongation, from 0.52 ± 0.11 μm/min in controls to -0.03 ± 0.08 μm/min.
source: However, ablation of the dorsal and ventral cells resulted in a significant reduction of the rate of new interface elongation over the subsequent 120 s of elongation, from 0.52 ± 0.11 μm/min in controls to -0.03 ± 0.08 μm/min (p = 0.01, Figure 3D–F).
evidence: This is an experimental finding with statistical analysis, supported by data in Figure 3D-F.

claim: In 3/5 vertices that resolved when dorsal/ventral cells were ablated, new DV edges formed but were not sustained beyond 1 min, collapsing back into vertices.
source: Notably, in 3/5 vertices that resolved when dorsal/ventral cells were ablated, new DV edges formed but were not sustained beyond 1 min, collapsing back into vertices.
evidence: This is an experimental observation from targeted laser ablation experiments.

claim: Dorsal/ventral cells are necessary to sustain the elongation of new DV interfaces, but not the resolution of multicellular vertices.
source: Together, our data suggest that dorsal/ventral cells are necessary to sustain the elongation of new DV interfaces, but not the resolution of multicellular vertices.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experiments disrupting contractility in dorsal/ventral cells.

claim: Upon wounding by irradiation with a UV laser, germband cells undergo apical constriction driven by medial-apical actomyosin networks.
source: Upon wounding by irradiation with a UV laser, germband cells undergo apical constriction driven by medial-apical actomyosin networks (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Apical constriction of germband cells generates ectopic tension on the surrounding cell interfaces.
source: Apical constriction of germband cells generates ectopic tension on the surrounding cell interfaces (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A, arrowheads).
evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Under sham-irradiation, the cell area and medial myosin of the anterior and posterior cells remained largely unaffected, and the new DV interface elongated at a rate of 0.79 ± 0.14 μm/min.
source: Under sham-irradiation (UV laser fully attenuated using a neutral density filter), the cell area and medial myosin of the anterior and posterior cells remained largely unaffected, and the new DV interface elongated at a rate of 0.79 ± 0.14 μm/min (Figure 4A,C,E).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from control experiments, supported by data in Figure 4A,C,E.

claim: When the cells anterior and posterior were irradiated with UV light, myosin accumulated on the apical surface of the wounded cells and their apical areas decreased rapidly.
source: Conversely, when the cells anterior and posterior were irradiated with UV light, myosin accumulated on the apical surface of the wounded cells and their apical areas decreased rapidly (Figure 4B,D)
evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by data in Figure 4B,D.

claim: Under ectopic tension parallel to the AP axis, new DV junctions elongated at a rate of 1.73 ± 0.30 μm/min, 2.1-fold faster than the elongation rate in controls.
source: Under ectopic tension parallel to the AP axis, new DV junctions elongated at a rate of 1.73 ± 0.30 μm/min, 2.1-fold faster than the elongation rate in controls (p = 6.2 × 10−3, Figure 4E).
evidence: This is an experimental finding with statistical analysis, supported by data in Figure 4E.

claim: Local mechanical tension parallel to the AP axis is sufficient to promote rapid assembly of new DV interfaces during vertex resolution in germband extension.
source: These results indicate that local mechanical tension parallel to the AP axis is sufficient to promote rapid assembly of new DV interfaces during vertex resolution in germband extension.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the ectopic tension experiments.

claim: All four-cell vertices examined in control embryos (n = 12) resolved within 30° of the AP axis.
source: All the four-cell vertices examined in control embryos (n = 12) resolved within 30° of the AP axis, and the rate of new interface assembly was 0.69 ± 0.13 μm/min (Figure 4F,H).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from control experiments, supported by data in Figure 4F,H.

claim: The rate of new interface assembly in control embryos was 0.69 ± 0.13 μm/min.
source: All the four-cell vertices examined in control embryos (n = 12) resolved within 30° of the AP axis, and the rate of new interface assembly was 0.69 ± 0.13 μm/min (Figure 4F,H).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from control experiments, supported by data in Figure 4F,H.

claim: When ectopic tension was applied along the DV axis, the rate of new edge elongation was not affected (0.74 ± 0.18 μm/min).
source: When we applied ectopic tension along the DV axis, the rate of new edge elongation was not affected (0.74 ± 0.18 μm/min, p = 0.8)
evidence: This is an experimental finding with statistical analysis.

claim: When ectopic tension was applied along the DV axis, the orientation of the new edge changed and occurred within 30° of the DV axis in 13 out of 13 cases.
source: When we applied ectopic tension along the DV axis, the rate of new edge elongation was not affected (0.74 ± 0.18 μm/min, p = 0.8), but the orientation of the new edge changed and occurred within 30° of the DV axis in 13 out of 13 cases (Figure 4G,H).
evidence: This is an experimental finding supported by data in Figure 4G,H.

claim: Local tension can promote and orient the assembly of new cell-cell interfaces.
source: Together, our data indicate that local tension can promote and orient the assembly of new cell-cell interfaces, suggesting a central role for mechanical forces during vertex resolution in Drosophila axis elongation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the ectopic tension experiments showing both acceleration and reorientation of vertex resolution.

claim: Mechanical forces play a central role during vertex resolution in Drosophila axis elongation.
source: Together, our data indicate that local tension can promote and orient the assembly of new cell-cell interfaces, suggesting a central role for mechanical forces during vertex resolution in Drosophila axis elongation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the combined experimental findings.

claim: Expression of inactive or constitutively active forms of myosin in embryos lacking the wild-type motor protein disrupts the directionality of vertex resolution during germband extension.
source: Consistent with this, expression of inactive or constitutively active forms of myosin in embryos lacking the wild-type motor protein disrupts the directionality of vertex resolution during germband extension (Kasza et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Mechanical tension is necessary for directional resolution of multicellular vertices in the mouse embryonic ectoderm during limb bud elongation.
source: Furthermore, mechanical tension is necessary for directional resolution of multicellular vertices in the mouse embryonic ectoderm during limb bud elongation (Lau et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: In the Drosophila dorsal thorax, actomyosin contractility in new edges is tightly regulated to facilitate their elongation.
source: In the Drosophila dorsal thorax, whose architecture is determined by neighbour exchange events, actomyosin contractility in new edges is tightly regulated to facilitate their elongation (Bardet et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The increase in tension on the new contact may be caused locally by the pulsatile, anisotropic contraction of the cells around the resolving vertex.
source: Our data suggest that the increase in tension on the new contact may be caused locally by the pulsatile, anisotropic contraction of the cells around the resolving vertex.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental findings showing correlation between cell contractions and edge elongation.

claim: Cells in the mouse limb bud ectoderm display pulsed contractions that are disrupted in β-catenin mutants.
source: Interestingly, cells in the mouse limb bud ectoderm also display pulsed contractions that are disrupted in β-catenin mutants, and in these mutants the directionality of vertex resolution is lost (Lau et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: In β-catenin mutants in the mouse limb bud ectoderm, the directionality of vertex resolution is lost.
source: Interestingly, cells in the mouse limb bud ectoderm also display pulsed contractions that are disrupted in β-catenin mutants, and in these mutants the directionality of vertex resolution is lost (Lau et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Pulsed contractile activity plays a general role in orienting and promoting cell intercalation.
source: Together, these results are consistent with a general role for pulsed contractile activity in orienting and promoting cell intercalation.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from comparing findings across different model systems.

claim: The anterior and posterior cells contribute to both vertex resolution and new edge elongation.
source: We find that anterior/posterior and dorsal/ventral cells may play different roles during multicellular vertex resolution. Our data suggest that the anterior and posterior cells contribute to both vertex resolution and new edge elongation
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the targeted laser ablation experiments.

claim: The dorsal and ventral cells are mainly necessary to support the elongation of the edge once the vertex has resolved.
source: Our data suggest that the anterior and posterior cells contribute to both vertex resolution and new edge elongation, while the dorsal and ventral cells are mainly necessary to support the elongation of the edge once the vertex has resolved.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the targeted laser ablation experiments.

claim: Mathematical modelling predicts that periodic actomyosin contractility in the medial-apical surface of anterior and posterior cells could drive the assembly of new edges during germband extension.
source: Recent mathematical modelling predicts that periodic actomyosin contractility in the medial-apical surface of anterior and posterior cells could drive the assembly of new edges during germband extension (Lan et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior computational modeling work.

claim: The pulsed contraction of the anterior and posterior cells could cause rapid membrane reorganization in the dorsal and ventral cells.
source: The pulsed contraction of the anterior and posterior cells could cause rapid membrane reorganization in the dorsal and ventral cells (Pramanik et al., 2009), facilitating the assembly of an actin scaffold (Pickering et al., 2013) and the formation of junctions.
evidence: This is a speculative mechanism supported by citations to prior work on membrane reorganization and actin scaffolds.

claim: Rapid membrane reorganization in dorsal and ventral cells could facilitate the assembly of an actin scaffold and the formation of junctions.
source: The pulsed contraction of the anterior and posterior cells could cause rapid membrane reorganization in the dorsal and ventral cells (Pramanik et al., 2009), facilitating the assembly of an actin scaffold (Pickering et al., 2013) and the formation of junctions.
evidence: This is a speculative mechanism supported by citations to prior work.

claim: An accumulation of filamentous actin is the first known step of vertex resolution.
source: An accumulation of filamentous actin is the first known step of vertex resolution (Blankenship et al., 2006)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Blocking actin polymerization results in multicellular vertices that do not resolve.
source: An accumulation of filamentous actin is the first known step of vertex resolution (Blankenship et al., 2006), and in this study, we found that blocking actin polymerization results in multicellular vertices that do not resolve.
evidence: This is an experimental finding from the Cytochalasin D experiments.

claim: Actin polymerization may play a central role in vertex resolution.
source: Thus, actin polymerization may play a central role in vertex resolution.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that blocking actin polymerization prevents vertex resolution.

claim: Mechanical forces can control actin dynamics in vitro, possibly by inducing conformational changes in the formin family of actin regulators to favour faster and more frequent polymerization of actin filaments.
source: Mechanical forces can control actin dynamics in vitro, possibly by inducing conformational changes in the formin family of actin regulators to favour faster and more frequent polymerization of actin filaments (Courtemanche et al., 2013; Higashida et al., 2013; Jegou et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior in vitro work.

claim: Actin filaments are less susceptible to severing in the presence of increased tension.
source: In addition, actin filaments are less susceptible to severing in the presence of increased tension (Hayakawa et al., 2011), which may accelerate actin assembly at nascent cell interfaces.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Reduced susceptibility of actin filaments to severing under tension may accelerate actin assembly at nascent cell interfaces.
source: In addition, actin filaments are less susceptible to severing in the presence of increased tension (Hayakawa et al., 2011), which may accelerate actin assembly at nascent cell interfaces.
